You Won't Believe How Much This BMW X5 Sold For – Spoiler Alert: Almost Nothing!
13 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
The previous two generation of the BMW X5 are some of the best-looking premium mid-size crossovers in their class, and this is my humble opinion. The second-gen has also aged quite nicely, and the original is definitely not bad at all either, and this one goes for nothing these days.
On average, you will have to fork out between $2,500 and over $17,000 for the E53, and the latter sum is for the V8-powered range-topper, and an example with decent mileage and in a very nice overall condition. Its successor, the E70, aka the second-gen, goes for roughly $3,500 to some $22,000, and paying the latter sum will get you a cool X5 M. The third-gen fetches between $11,000 and over $35,000, and the from $25,000 to over $75,000.
As for the pictured BMW X5, it is an F15 2015 model year , and that places it in the third generation that was assembled between 2013 and 2018. Production took place in the United States of America, at the South Carolina plant, and this model was also put together in Russia, Egypt, Malaysia, and Indonesia. It shared its nuts and bolts with the era’s X6, as well as the G30 5 Series, G32 6 Series, G11 7 Series, and G15 8 series, among others.
This machine is presented in Glacier Silver Metallic on top of a black interior, and was located in Miami, Florida, prior to it changing hands recently. We will get to this part in a few moments, as first, we have to delve into some of the details, like the powertrain. You see, this is an xDrive35d model, which means that it comes with a diesel engine.
Photo: Cars&Bids The mill is none other than the N57 3.0-liter straight-six turbodiesel , which was officially good for 255 hp (258 ps/190 kW) at 4,000 rpm and 413 lb-ft (560 Nm) of torque available between 1,500 and 3,000 rpm. It features an 8-speed automatic transmission, and all-wheel drive, and independent tests back in the day revealed that it took a little over 7 seconds to accelerate from 0-60 mph (0-97 kph). The top speed is electronically capped at 130 mph (210 kph).
This diesel-powered BMW X5 features 19-inch wheels, has running boards, a panoramic sunroof, a rearview camera, a Harman Kardon premium sound system, Dakota leather upholstery, and power-adjustable and heated front seats. These are all mentioned in the listing, just like the known flaws, which are the chips and scratches on the outside, some curb rash on the wheels, and wear on the seats.
According to the ad, the crossover in question had its engine oil and filter changed in March 2025, when the odometer read 72,731 miles (117,049 km). The engine oil and filter were also changed in March 2024, at 68,215 miles (109,781 km), which is also when the brake fluid was flushed. In February 2023, at 64,742 miles (104,192 km), this X5 paid another visit to the shop, and also in February 2023, for new front brake pads, and a new fuel filter, among others, at 60,994 miles (98,160 km).
Photo: Cars&Bids The only reported modification revolves around the windows, which have been tinted, and the new owner should also know that the tires carry 2023 and 2024 date codes. Besides the BMW X5 in question, the new owner will also get an OEM bike rack, a set of rubber floor mats, a cargo mat, the owner’s manual, and a single key. The vehicle had 79,000 miles (~127,100 km) on the clock at the time of cataloging, a clean Florida title, and a clean Carfax history report.
The selling dealer reportedly bought this machine earlier in 2026, and they listed for grabs on Cars&Bids as part of an auction that ended a few days ago. The gavel hit the table on October 20, 2026, and this BMW X5 failed to change hands. However, it did sell after the online auction ended, and the price was $15,800. And given that we mentioned the market value of this model above, you know that that sum is basically average.
It is also nothing compared to what this ride initially cost, as it sold from just under $60K, excluding options, and dealer fees. And for what it’s worth, it is definitely a lot of car for the money, not to mention that this one features quite a few goodies, looks very good both inside and out for something that was made over a decade ago, and has aged very nicely, which is something that we probably won’t be able to say about the new-age Neue Klasse BMW X5, namely the G65 (the G78 is the LWB for China).
Would you have picked up this BMW X5 for just under $16K if you came across the ad in time? I probably would have, but then again, I also dig the model in question, the powertrain, and the spec of this car. You can check it out in more detail here .

This Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio Was Over $100K New and Just Sold for Toyota Prius Money
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
Just like its four-door sibling, the Giulia sports sedan , the Alfa Romeo Stelvio refuses to die. Well, for now, anyway, because the Italian company is currently working on the successors of both models.
Production of the crossover started back in 2016, and in 2023, it received a mid-cycle refresh. The model is offered with a straight-four turbocharged mill, a four-pot diesel, and a V6 gasoline engine, and the latter is reserved for the range-topping version of the series, namely the Quadrifoglio. This mill boasts plenty of Ferrari DNA, as you likely know, and it is the mill that powers the Stelvio pictured above.
The 2.9-liter twin-turbocharged V6 engine was originally good for 505 horsepower (512 ps/377 kW ) and 443 pound-feet (600 Nm) of torque, directed to the all-wheel drive system through an eight-speed automatic transmission. The Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio hits 60 mph (97 kph) in just 3.6 seconds, and goes up to 177 mph (285 kph) before running out of breath. The Jaguar F-Pace SVR, Mercedes-AMG GLC 63, BMW X3 M, and Porsche Macan Turbo were some of its rivals in the premium compact super crossover class.
This Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio is a 2019 model year, with a Circuito Gray Matte exterior, and a black and red cockpit. It rides on 20-inch wheels backed up by Brembo carbon ceramic brakes, a a dynamic dual-mode exhaust system, carbon fiber grille and door mirror casings, and adaptive cruise control with stop and go function. Additional gizmos mentioned in the listing include the panoramic sunroof, power-adjustable and heated front seats, Harman Kardon audio system, leather and Alcantara upholstery, and carbon trim.
Photo: Cars&Bids The Italian super crossover in question has a clean Pennsylvania title, was located in La Jolla, California before it changed hands, has never been involved in an accident, had 37,700 miles (60,700 km) under its belt at the time of cataloging, and was listed for grabs by its first and only owner. The man bought it new in January 2020, paying $105,735 for it, according to the attached window sticker, and he recently parted ways with it.
According to the ad, some of the known flaws include a tear in the left rear door weatherstripping, some creases on the driver’s seat outer bolster, and scratches on the rear bumper. The Carfax report shows two owners, though the seller noted that a new title was issued when the vehicle was moved to California. This Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio had its engine oil and filter changed earlier this year, in June 2026, when the odometer read 36,198 miles (58,255 km).
The engine oil and filter were also changed in April 2025 at 27,856 miles (44,830 km), and a maintenance inspection was performed, one tire was mounted in October 2023, at 21,038 miles (33,857 km), and the brake fluid was flushed, four tires were mounted, and the engine oil and filter were changed in September 2023, at 20,708 miles (33,326 km). In December 2022, four tires were mounted, and the coolant was flushed, and the car had 16,308 miles (26,245 km) on the odo then.
Photo: Cars&Bids Mind you, this is not the usual Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio either, because you are looking at #32 of 55 NRING Edition examples made for North America, hence while it features some extra goodies over the rest of the lineup. This model is currently worth between $32,000 and $42,000 in today’s used car market in the United States of America, so depreciation has hit it like a train, given that it used to have an MSRP of almost $100,000 originally.
The pictured 2019 Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio NRING Edition was advertised at the excitement of no reserve on Cars&Bids, as part of an online auction that recently concluded. When the gavel hit the table, this super crossover ended up changing hands for $34,760, which is similar to a new Toyota Prius Plug-in Hybrid, as the 2027 model year kicks off at $33,980, excluding destination, options, and dealer fees.
This means that the owner lost $61,975 in almost seven years due to depreciation alone, or a little over $1.6 every mile. Alfa Romeo’s Stelvio Quadrifoglio is definitely a lot of car for the money, regardless of whether we are talking about the NRING Edition or not, and given that the value of this thing has gone down significantly, this is probably a good time to finally buy one. You know, assuming that you are into this model, and we reckon you are, otherwise you probably wouldn’t have stuck around this much.
But if you came across this particular Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quadrifoglio , and it had a $34,760 sticker price attached to it, would you have bought it? Keep in mind that it has been owned by the same person since new, does not have any issues other than a few visual ones, and the odo read a very decent 37,700 miles at the time of cataloging. You can check out the listing here .

Chart of the Week: Contract Rate Change Direction Index – USA SONAR : CRCD.USA
Shippers who have reset truckload contracts over the past several months are paying about 13% more than the rates they replaced. That is the reading from SONAR’s new Contract Rate Change Direction index (CRCD.USA), which stood at 13.11% on Oct. 22, up from 3.53% a year earlier.
This index measures the average percentage difference between a new contract base rate and the one it replaced within an established shipper-carrier relationship. It counts a change only when the old rate had held steady for more than 90 days, which filters out short-term noise and isolates true bid-cycle repricing. The index is a seven-day rolling average, updated daily.
The metric strips out the effects of temporary route guide waterfalling and contract-plus pricing to show more durable changes in rates. Route guide failures say a lot about market pressure, but the rates they produce can overstate what eventually becomes the sustained cost.
It is also important to note that the index measures only contracts that are changing. That makes it largely agnostic to volume, and readings can thin out when few contracts are changing. CRCD also does not account for whether a carrier moves up or down in a shipper’s routing guide after a rate change. That gap showed up in 2025: contract resets ran at roughly 3% to 4% starting in late 2024, yet the average contract rate index (VCRPM1) showed flat to slightly lower invoiced rates through most of the year.
Pairing the two indexes shows how successful carriers’ rate increases have been, or not. CRCD leads invoice data directionally, but it does not predict whether increases will stick. That carriers were pushing for increases a year before the recent cycle turned should be a cautionary tale for shippers now navigating a period of extreme rate inflation.
The current 13% reading shows that most contract changes are now landing well into the double digits, nearly a year after tender rejection rates jumped above 9%. As the chart above shows, contract rate changes lag rejection rates, which suggests it takes a sustained period of elevated rejections before contract rate increases follow. With rejection rates averaging close to 13% over the past few months, increases are still coming in above 10%. Note that CRCD is not an annualized rate. It measures the average change in contracts when they move, and a change does not register until it is implemented.
The takeaway for shippers is that carriers are still securing strong rate increases, and the contract rate index (VCRPM1) suggests those increases are sticking. The average increase should moderate as carriers move onto more financially healthy contracts. However, both FMCSA and tender data suggest capacity has not grown meaningfully over the past 12 months despite elevated rates, so it may take time for the curve to flatten.
About the Chart of the Week
The FreightWaves Chart of the Week is a chart selection from SONAR that provides an interesting data point to describe the state of the freight markets. A chart is chosen from thousands of potential charts on SONAR to help participants visualize the freight market in real time. Each week a Market Expert will post a chart, along with commentary, live on the front page. After that, the Chart of the Week will be archived on FreightWaves.com for future reference.
SONAR aggregates data from hundreds of sources, presenting the data in charts and maps and providing commentary on what freight market experts want to know about the industry in real time.
The FreightWaves data science and product teams are releasing new datasets each week and enhancing the client experience.

This Jeep Wrangler Kaizer Edition Costs Less Than You Probably Think
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | soflocustoms4x4
Believe it or not, the latest generation Jeep Wrangler will turn ten next year. Production of the JL commenced in November 2017, at the Toledo factory in Ohio, and it has been given a mid-cycle refresh for the 2024 model year.
The punchy machine has received plenty of attention from the gearhead crowd over the years, and even if it is not exactly fresh anymore, it still makes headlines today. It’s either a tuned example that usually gets our attention, or one that is searching for a new home in the United States of America. And this is a case of both, as the pictured machine has been visited by the tuning fairy, and it is for sale as we speak.
SoFlo Customs is the tuner behind it, and the project is called the Kaizer Edition. Why is that? Because it features a Kaiser M715 -inspired front end. This model was also called the “Five Quarter,” and in case you forgot, we are talking about an American light military truck that was based on the original Jeep Gladiator. The Kaiser M715 was made in Ohio from 1967 to 1969, and during this time, it is estimated that over 30,000 examples saw the light of day, packing a straight-six engine, a four-speed manual transmission, and four-wheel drive.
Truth be told, the pictured Jeep Wrangler rocks the Kaiser M715-inspired front fascia like a champ, this writer believes. And if you feel like you have seen design somewhere before, but you cannot put your finger on it, then you probably remember the Kaizer Edition version of the Jeep Gladiator that we wrote about last summer. That one was a lot more monstrous looking, and just like this Wrangler, it featured plenty of modifications, and was searching for a new home online back then.
Photo: Instagram | soflocustoms4x4 This Jeep Wrangler features an Army Green Kevlar paint finish on the outside, sits on 20-inch five-spoke bronze Apocalypse wheels that have been shod in 37-inch Ridge Blade tires for enhanced grip, and also benefits from a 4-inch (100+ mm) lift kit. SoFlo Customs also mentions the 2.5-inch diameter heavy-duty monotube shocks, the front and rear upgraded trackbars, geometry relocation kit, adjustable control arms, heavy-duty steering stabilizer, and solid aluminum bump stops.
Besides these features, the modded Wrangler in question has a Mojave-style hood, a color-matched Baja front bumper with integrated LED spotlights, a new rear bumper, power retractable side steps, dedicated headlights with custom illumination, color-matched factory fender flares, cube lights with brackets for enhanced visibility off the beaten path, and a few other things that help it stand out from the crowd very easily.
Additional gizmos include the SoFlo King Ranch brown and black diamond-style leather interior, the 12-inch infotainment system, power door locks and windows, a reversing camera, and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. These are all mentioned on the tuner’s official website, alongside the powertrain, which is a 2.0-liter four-cylinder turbocharged unit rated at 270 hp (274 ps/201 kW) and 295 lb-ft (400 Nm) of torque, and paired with an eight-speed auto ‘box and four-wheel drive.
Photo: Instagram | soflocustoms4x4 Even though it is listed as a used vehicle, the pictured Jeep Wrangler is actually a brand new ride, as its odometer read only 61 miles (98 km) at the time of cataloging. SoFlo Customs says that this is a 2026 model year machine, and it is located in West Palm Beach, Florida, in case you want to check it out in person before making the big step. However, we’d recommend getting in touch with the vendor, which is the tuner, if you plan to see this ride in the flesh.
What else should you know about it? That the asking price excludes tax, tag, title, and other official fees, and includes the $1,398 shop supply fee, and the $349 tag processing fee. But how much must one fork out if they want to buy this 2026 Jeep Wrangler Kaizer Edition? That would be $67,499.99, as this was the asking price at the time of writing. And to be honest, judging by the aggressive makeover, as well as other work that has gone into it, we initially thought that it would be much more than that.
That kind of money would get you a nice Rubicon X 2027 model year Jeep Wrangler straight from the dealer, with only the delivery miles under its belt. The Willys 392 requires spending a minimum of $70,995, and the Moab 392 has an MSRP of $79,995. The lesser Sahara, Smoky Mountain, Rewind, Rubicon, Willys, and Sport S start at $51,410, $50,545, $49,380, $47,130, $43,230, and $39,035, respectively, whereas the base Sport can be had from $36,635.
Now, if you feel like this modded Jeep Wrangler is worth the asking price, and you want to make it yours, then you should reach out to the tuner to discuss the details. But do you really dig this Kaiser-inspired makeover? View this post on Instagram A post shared by SoFlo Customs (@soflocustoms4x4)

Electric scooters have carried just about everything at this point, from commuters and tourists to groceries and probably more than a few ill-advised passengers. But two riders in Charlotte, North Carolina, may have just raised the bar after police stopped them cruising down the street on an actual couch apparently powered by a pair of Lime electric scooters.
Officers with the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department encountered the unusual contraption traveling down South Tryon Street, according to a recent post shared by the department.
“Well, this was certainly a first,” police wrote. “Our EDU Officers encountered quite the situation this weekend when they stopped two gentlemen traveling down S. Tryon Street on a couch… Yes, an actual couch.”
From the photo, the setup appears to consist of a full-size sofa perched across two Lime shared electric scooters. Exactly how the scooters were attached – or how steering was accomplished – isn’t clear. But judging by the fact that the riders apparently made it far enough to attract police attention, the system seems to have worked at least reasonably well with some coordinated efforts by the dual pilots.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
And frankly, as someone who has famously seen and operated plenty of bizarre electric vehicles over the years, I have to give some points for creativity here.
Police seemed to feel similarly, though they were understandably less enthusiastic about the safety implications of piloting living-room furniture down a public street.
“While we appreciate the creativity, we do have to remind everyone: no matter what you’re ‘driving’ (using that term extremely loosely), please think about safety first,” the department wrote.
Police also joked that it was “probably best to leave the mobile furniture displays to IKEA.”
It isn’t clear whether either rider was cited or arrested, and police didn’t publicly identify the pair.
But while a two-scooter electric couch probably isn’t the micromobility revolution cities had in mind, you’ve got to admit: door-to-door transportation doesn’t get much more comfortable than this.

1959 Piaggio Vespa 400 Is Not a Scooter, but a Rare Microcar
14 photos
Photo: eBay/Premier Auto Group of South Florida
Built by Piaggio, the Vespa is perhaps the world's most iconic scooter brand. First introduced in 1946, the Vespa scooter is still around today, retaining the design that made the original popular. But did you know that the Vespa badge also found its way on a car?
It happened in 1957, when Piaggio joined the microcar market. The first microcars emerged in the years following World War II, with several companies jumping on the bandwagon in the early 1950s. By 1953, Iso had debuted the Isetta, which was later licensed by BMW, while Messerschmitt had launched the KR175. The Fuldamobil was introduced in 1950.
Piaggio reportedly started working on its microcar in 1952, but the production model didn't arrive until 1957, the same year when Fiat launched the more iconic 500. Piaggio called it the Vespa 400. But unlike the scooter, the microcar was produced by ACMA in France.
Smaller but just as charming as the Fiat 500 , the Vespa 400 was shaped like a two-door sedan and measured only 112 inches (2,850 mm) long. The 66.7-inch (1,693 mm) wheelbase provided room for two seats, but the passenger cabin could also accommodate two small children on the optional cushion. The tiny vehicle tipped the scales at only 790 pounds (360 kg).
Unsurprisingly, the Vespa 400 was fitted with a two-stroke two-cylinder engine. The 400cc engine delivered 13 horsepower in its early configuration, with output increased to 14 horsepower later on. The microcar was able to reach up to 55 mph (89 kph).
The Vespa 400 was pretty popular at first, selling 12,130 units in 1958. However, sales dropped to around 8,700 examples in 1959 and declined dramatically in 1960. Piaggio discontinued the model in 1961, with a total production of nearly 31,000 units. Most of these cars were sold in France. Nearly 1,700 examples crossed the pond to the United States.
The Vespa 400 is quite rare today, as most of these microcars were abandoned in disrepair. Restored examples are hard to come by, which is why this 1959 Vespa that surfaced in Pompano Beach, Florida, is a spectacular find.
For sale via Premier Auto Group, this Piaggio was restored about 10 years ago. The Narvik Blue paint is flawless, while the interior, albeit very sparse, is factory correct and amazingly clean.
Interestingly, this Vespa 400 wasn't sold in the US. The vehicle was actually delivered new in France and made the trip to North America sometime later. There's no info on whether it was restored before or after it made it into the US. The car has a four-speed manual gearbox, which was only available in European markets. This Vespa 400 is technically a GT model.
How much to take this tiny two-seater home? The dealership is asking $37,500 , but it's also accepting offers. It may sound like a lot for such a small vehicle, but some examples have actually fetched more at public auction in recent years.
The most expensive Vespa 400 changed hands for the equivalent of $42,000 in 2020. Back in 2011, another one sold for $41,250 at Amelia Island. In 2025, a 1959 version like this one traded for $40,320 in Arizona.

Photo: jonsibal / Instagram
Earlier this month, the Japanese automaker Mazda’s local division, Mazda North American Operations (MNAO), reported its best-ever September sales results: 34,519 deliveries, jumping no less than 32% compared to last year. Alas, the picture isn’t as rosy as it seems.
Just like AI chatbots like to package the so-called truth as if they’re politicians but if you’re a little educated, you can see right through their façade, Mazda actually needs to claw back to a positive performance during the final quarter of the year to come out of the woods. That’s because year-to-date sales totaled 310,268 units, which is actually almost three percent less than during the first nine months of last year.
Anyway, they’re doing okay with some of their older models, revealing that it’s sometimes better to play with your old toys rather than give in to the latest marketing stunts from those who want to sell you more expensive things. They’re a good example: the tried-and-true Mazda3 series jumped over 42% during the nine-month period, the MX-5 Miata was also up by more than 4%, and the CX-50 rose almost 20%, breathing down the neck of the all-new CX-5 by less than 1k units!
Meanwhile, the newer CX-70 and CX-90 are both down more than 21% compared to last year, and the latest rumor across the mill says that Mazda is ready to retire the CX-70 from the US market in 2027, with the two-row CX-90 taking over in its place. As such, are we surprised that even the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators have stopped dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI to take a virtual look at the older Mazdas?
Influential automotive virtual artist Jon Sibal, titled "jonsibal" on social media, usually plays with Japanese-style cars, so we're not surprised at all that he is thinking that now is maybe the perfect time to play with a CGI MX-5 Miata, showcasing his latest unofficial, hypothetical design project as if he’s ready to embark on a trial to reach the starting roster of the 2027 edition of the iconic Pikes Peak International Hillclimb, which next year is celebrating its 105th edition.
Of course, that’s not necessarily the target, as the author himself explains.
Instead, his “slightly modified” Miata ND (the model code for the fourth iteration) is actually a widebody, slammed version of the affordable sports car inspired by the JGTC competition – aka All Japan Grand Touring Car Championship, a grand touring car racing series created in 1993 and originally named the Zen Nihon GT Senshuken, which then changed to Super GT in 2005.
By the way, he says that he’s still working on “a few more details but should be done with it soon,” so we might see additional variants of the bonkers project soon enough. No worries, we’ll keep you posted! View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jon Sibal (@jonsibal)

Ferrari's Iconic F40 Gets a Modern Redesign in Fantasy Land, Purists May Want To Look Away
10 photos
Photo: Instagram | onb.artdesign
The Ferrari F40 is one of those supercars that needs no introduction. It was the last Prancing Horse approved by Enzo himself, and it is an icon that costs more than the proverbial arm and leg, as you are looking at a true collector’s item.
Assembled between 1987 and 1996, this model was offered as a two-door coupe, with a longitudinally-mounted rear mid-engine, and rear-wheel drive layout. And like all other great machines from that era, it had a manual transmission that channeled the output and thrust to the rear wheels. The engine was a V8, and one with twin turbocharging, in case you forgot, and while the power produced may be pretty much nothing these days, let’s not forget that we are talking about a machine that was developed in the ‘80s.
On top of that, the Ferrari F40 may have less power than some of today’s new-age vehicles, but the thrills it provides are unmatched. How much oomph are we looking at? That would be 471 brake horsepower, equaling 352 kilowatts and 478 metric horsepower, and 426 pound-feet (577 Nm) of torque. The quarter mile took only 11.9 seconds, it had a maximum speed of 201 mph (324 kph), and from 0 to 62 mph (0-100 kph), it needed just 4.1 seconds.
The analog classic supercar that preceded the 288 GTO was 77.6 inches (1,970 mm) long, 44.3 inches (1,124 mm) tall, and 77.6 inches (1,970 mm) wide. It had a 96.5-inch long (2,450 mm) wheelbase, and had a curb weight of only 2,765 pounds (1,254 kg) for the Euro-spec, whereas the US model weighed a hair over 3,000 pounds (1,369 kg.). By comparison, the F80, which is its modern-day successor, weighs 3,362 pounds (1,525 kg) dry.
Photo: Instagram | onb.artdesign Ferrari’s F40 design is definitely iconic, and we can safely say that this model has aged like fine wine. Nevertheless, there are few examples out there that have been visited by the tuning fairy, and the one pictured above is one of them. Actually, it was the virtual tuning fairy that paid a visit to this one, because, as mentioned in the title, it is not a real example, as it lives in Fantasy Land, courtesy of its creator, @onb.artdesign on Instagram.
The pixel artist decided to imagine this iconic supercar with a slightly more modern design, and that’s why it features different headlights, a new hood at the front, and a new bumper with larger vents. It also has new mirrors that have been virtually repositioned, as well as new side skirts skirts, and side windows that remind us of racers. The back end features a pair of light strips on each side, which are the new taillights, replacing the original round lighting units.
The bumper is a lot flatter this time around, there are no visible reflectors integrated into it, and the three central-mounted exhaust tips are significantly larger. There is also a diffuser attached to the rear bumper, and a much larger wing that seems to be adjustable. The ground clearance is pretty much the same as before, and the wheels are new. These are larger, have a five-spoke design, and have clearly come from the aftermarket world .
Photo: Instagram | onb.artdesign This virtually-reimagined Ferrari F40 has a blue paint finish on the outside, the usual Prancing Horse logos at the front, sides, and rear, and the new alloys have a chrome look, just like the fresh exhaust tips. There are also some black elements here and there, and we can see that the interior is also black, with red five-point racing harnesses. A half-cage is also on deck for safety purposes, and we want to say that everything else carries over, but the truth is that we do not know.
That’s because the rendering artist behind these digital illustrations hasn’t opened up the door, so your guess is as good as ours whether this CGI-infused machine may or may not have other modern features on the inside. And to be honest, if we did not know anything about the Ferrari F40 , we’d say that this thing is definitely on the cool side of things. But since we are talking about one of the coolest Ferraris ever made, we (or I in this case) do not necessarily approve of the makeover.
And speaking of cool Prancing Horses, besides the F40, these include the 288 GTO, the F40, the Enzo, and the LaFerrari. Ferrari’s F40 is now a multi-million dollar affair, as it is typically worth from $3.5 to over 6 million dollars, and one example sold for a record-breaking $8.3+ million a couple of months ago at auction.
But do you actually like the way this rendered Ferrari F40 looks? We promise we can still be friends if you say yes, so feel free to speak your mind about it in the comments area below. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Onur Bakır (@onb.artdesign)

This Affordable, Cabin-Like Camper Van Is a Full-Time Home on Wheels for a Retired Adventurer
14 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / CheapRVliving
Camper vans can take so many different forms – although most of the projects we've covered here on autoevolution have all-out luxurious setups, I also enjoy sharing simpler and cheaper builds that are more attainable to a regular Joe – with some creativity, you'd be surprised by how practical such a build can be. That's the type of rig I'd like to share with you today.
What we have here is a mobile home based on a 2021 Ram ProMaster 2500. It was converted by Steve, and he has been using it as a full-time home for more than five years. Even after all this time, Steve still recommends the nomadic lifestyle – he shared that he is retired and lives off his pension and social security.
Steve has a clear reason why he chose the ProMaster : price - it's most likely the determining factor of purchase for most people. He bought it brand-new toward the end of the pandemic and it took him about a year to complete the build. What's more, he shared that he gets about 16 MPG (14.7 L/100km).
As usual, let's start by taking a look at the exterior. It rides on Black Rhino wheels wrapped in BFGoodrich KO3 all-terrain tires. To be able to better handle going off the beaten path, Steve installed a 3-inch (7-centimeter) lift for the suspension. The tires offer an extra inch of lift.
A ladder at the back lets you quickly and easily climb on top of the rig. There, you'll come across a Fiamma F45S awning and a 400 W solar array. Furthermore, Steve fitted a swing-away bike carrier to the rear hitch.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / CheapRVliving Other notable mods are a guard for the motor, a T-Vent window on the sliding door, and two rear windows.
Enter, and you'll be greeted by a homey, welcoming interior. It has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space.
This setup allows you to use the cabin as a seating area not just while driving but also after you've parked. The driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases, allowing you to turn them around to face the back of the van.
The passenger seat base houses a Webasto heater that's tapped directly into the vehicle's fuel tank. What's more, you'll find a sizeable headliner shelf above, perfect for storing bits and bobs.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / CheapRVliving Steve opted for a warm, cabin-like design – it consists of sage green birch plywood cabinetry with pine elements, wood walls with a matching ceiling, and wood flooring with rugs on top. Moreover, Steve used Thinsulate to insulate the walls and ceiling, and also added Kilmat to sound-deaden the van.
The first part of the living space is the kitchen, which is split into two units, one on each side. It features two butcher block countertops, a 12V Isotherm fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, and a deep stainless steel sink with a cutting board cover.
Four overhead cabinets, four drawers, and a cabinet underneath the sink are available for storage. The latter hides a 7-gallon (26-liter) canister that acts as a greywater tank for the sink. Speaking of plumbing, the van is also equipped with a 20-gallon (76-liter) freshwater tank mounted underneath the bed.
Finally, the rear part of the living space is taken up by the bedroom. Steve built the bed platform to accommodate a full-size bed arranged east to west. He used thin slats, on top of which he added a mattress that's 6 inches (15 centimeters) thick.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / CheapRVliving The bedroom also boasts four overhead cabinets (two on each side), a swiveling fan, two reading lights, and a Maxxair ceiling vent fan.
Underneath the bedroom, Steve created a massive garage that's accessible from both inside and outside the van. To make use of the space as best as possible, Steve stores a lot of his items in plastic bins.
The garage also houses a Luggable Loo camping toilet for emergencies and a propane canister that Steve uses for a portable camping stove. For safety, he installed a smoke and carbon dioxide detector.
The electrical system's highlights are a 305 Ah battery bank and a 3,000 W inverter. The more impressive bit is that he built the system himself with no prior experience, albeit he did buy the system from a company and he had to connect everything – that's still not a beginner-friendly task. He can use two charging sources to keep the battery bank topped off: shore power and solar power .
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / CheapRVliving All in all, Steve created a wonderful home on wheels without having any prior experience with woodworking or any other parts of building camper vans. Considering he had to learn as he went, his conversion turned out amazing. Even though he didn't share a total cost, I'm sure the project was affordable.
